source.version: Published conference paper (version of record): Creativity and Cognition (C&C '24), June 23-26, 2024, Chicago, IL, USA, ACM, pp. 413-425, https://doi.org/10.1145/3635636.3656204, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
source.title_on_document: Homogenization Effects of Large Language Models on Human Creative Ideation

paper_design_summary: Within-subjects user study: each participant did four 8-minute divergent ideation prompts (two TTCT-style Product Improvement and two Improbable Consequences prompts), two with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and two with a web version of the Oblique Strategies card deck, with the order of tools and prompts randomized per participant and balanced. 33 of 36 recruited participants were analyzed. Ideas were scored for group-level and individual-level semantic divergence (sentence embeddings), fluency, flexibility (hand-coded categories), elaboration (stoplisted word count), and originality (unique ideas); self-reports covered responsibility and the Creativity Support Index.

studies.label: Within-subjects user study: ChatGPT vs Oblique Strategies deck on TTCT-style ideation prompts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two creativity support tools (ChatGPT, Oblique Strategies deck) and of the ideation prompts; every participant used both tools, two prompts each.
assignment.quote: The order of CSTs and prompts was randomized per participant and balanced across the entire experiment.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 416), Section 3.3 Procedure; also PDF p. 3 (p. 415), Section 3: 'We conducted a within-subjects experiment'

arms.name: ChatGPT
arms.description: Ideation with ChatGPT 3.5 (May 3, 2023 or August 3, 2023 release) on two of the four prompts.

arms.name: Oblique Strategies (OS)
arms.description: Ideation with a web app version of the Oblique Strategies card deck (non-AI creativity support tool, the paper's control condition) on the other two prompts.

participants.exclusions: 36 participants originally recruited; 3 excluded from all analyses for failure to follow directions (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted). The paper says 'originally recruited', not 'randomized'; both arms are the same people (within-subjects). Some process/self-report numbers use 36 as denominator (e.g., CSI t(35); 72.22%, n = 26).
participants.who: Adults aged 22-44 (M = 28.36) recruited from academic mailing lists, forums, and social media: 12 students, 10 creative professionals, 11 other professionals; sessions remote-moderated over videoconference; $17.50 gift card for a one-hour session.
participants.country: not_stated (Santa Clara University IRB; remote sessions)
participants.quote: Of the 36 participants originally recruited, three were excluded from all analyses for failure to follow direction (e.g., not using ChatGPT when prompted to do so).
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (p. 415), Section 3.1.1; PDF p. 4 (p. 416), Section 3.1.2 ('Our sample included 33 participants')

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT 3.5 (versions released May 3, 2023, n = 6, and August 3, 2023, n = 30)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used ChatGPT freely while generating ideas for the prompt; most (86.11%, n = 31) pasted the ideation prompt into ChatGPT; some copied output directly, some paraphrased, some combined (Sections 4.5.2-4.5.3).

task.description: Four divergent-thinking prompts based on the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Product Improvement (stuffed toy animal; jigsaw puzzle) and Improbable Consequences (great fog; weak gravity). Participants generated as many ideas as they could and tried to think of ideas no one else would.
task.duration: 8 minutes per ideation prompt; one-hour session

outcomes.name: Group-level homogenization: divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all participant ideas for that task
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each idea to the average embedding of all participant ideas for the prompt, expressed as divergence (higher = less homogeneous); embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (SentenceTransformers), validated against human categories in Appendix A (58.92% average agreement). Paired comparison over 33 participants.

contrasts.reported: ChatGPT (M = .24, SD = .07) vs OS (M = .28, SD = .08), t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47, 95% CI [.00,.07]. Lower divergence = more homogeneous with ChatGPT (sign reversed relative to diversity: ChatGPT less diverse).

diversity_detail.metric: Divergence from the average embedding (cosine-similarity based) of all participant ideas for the same prompt, averaged per participant
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the centroid (average embedding) of all participant ideas for that prompt; the paper does not say whether the centroid pools both conditions
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Paired t-test over 33 participants (t(32)); 95% CI; figure error bars use Cousineau-Morey within-subject correction
diversity_detail.notes: Paper calls this RQ1 and its 'primary homogenization analysis' uses this embedding model (PDF p. 12, Appendix A). Higher value = more diverse, so ChatGPT is less diverse across people.

outcomes.name: Individual-level homogenization: divergence of each idea from the average embedding of the same participant's other ideas for the prompt
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Semantic divergence of each idea from the average embedding of all other ideas the same participant generated for the same prompt (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Within-person variety, so coded flexibility per codebook. Text values (.65/.66) differ from Figure 3 axis values (about .33-.35); see open_questions.

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of idea categories (hand-coded)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Grounded-theory coding produced 181 idea categories from 1271 responses; count of categories hit by each participant; coders blind to condition.

outcomes.name: Fluency: simple idea count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas generated; paper describes about one additional idea, approximately a 15% increase, with ChatGPT. Paper does not state whether the count is per prompt or per tool.

outcomes.name: Elaboration: stoplisted word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed word count of each idea excluding a stoplist of common filler words (no form code for word counts; automated_score is the closest). Printed p = 0.237 looks inconsistent with t(32) = 2.32 and a CI excluding zero; see open_questions.

outcomes.name: Originality: number of unique ideas (ideas no other participant generated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of a participant's ideas that no other participant in the sample generated (based on the hand-coded categories). Robustness variants, same conclusion: (a) unique responses at a 5% threshold: ChatGPT (M = .87, SD = .88) vs OS (M = .90, SD = 1.07), t(32) = .134, p = 0.894, d = .02, 95% CI [-.34,.39]; (b) weighted flexibility score (each category weighted by its frequency in the sample): ChatGPT (M = 6.34, SD = 3.31) vs OS (M = 5.50, SD = 3.01), t(32) = 1.424, p = 0.164, d = .26, 95% CI [-.35,2.02].

outcomes.name: Sense of responsibility for the ideas (self-report)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Percent of responsibility participants assigned to themselves versus the tool. Self-report; does not meet criterion 3. Listed for completeness.

outcomes.name: Creativity Support Index (self-report)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: CSI questionnaire after each tool; no differences on subscales (Exploration, Engagement, Effort/Reward Tradeoff, Tool Transparency, Expressiveness). Self-report; does not meet criterion 3. Note t(35), implying 36 participants.

company_involvement.description: Funded by Hackworth Grant GR102981 from the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics; no company authors or company funding stated.

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomized order of ChatGPT versus a non-AI tool (Oblique Strategies) meets criterion 1, and outcomes are scored on the ideas (embedding divergence, idea counts, categories, word count), meeting criterion 3. But only 33 people were analyzed (36 recruited), below the 50-participant threshold, so it is a small randomized experiment listed in the screening report only. The codebook (Section 13) names this paper as excluded by the 50-participant rule.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT, 33 participants' ideas were less divergent from the group's average embedding than with the Oblique Strategies deck (M = .24 vs .28, t(32) = 2.154, p = 0.038, d = .47; PDF p. 5, Section 4.1.2), with no individual-level difference, while fluency, flexibility, and elaboration were higher (PDF p. 6).
open_questions: Individual-level divergence: text reports ChatGPT M = .65 vs OS M = .66 (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1.3), but Figure 3's y-axis shows means near .33-.35 for 'Divergence (From Self)'. The text values may be similarity (1 minus divergence); the paper does not say.
Elaboration: printed p = 0.237 with t(32) = 2.32 and 95% CI [.22,3.37] (PDF p. 6, Section 4.3.3); the p-value looks like a typo, but the form records it as printed.

Participant counts vary: 33 analyzed in the outcome tests (t(32)), but the CSI test reports t(35) and several process percentages use 36 as the denominator (e.g., 72.22%, n = 26; 86.11%, n = 31; ChatGPT version n = 6 and n = 30).
The paper does not say whether the group-level centroid pools ideas from both conditions or is computed within condition.
Fluency means (8.39 vs 7.32) are not labeled per prompt or per tool (two prompts per tool); 1271 total ideas is reported for the full study.
notes: Section 4.5 reports non-randomized process comparisons within the ChatGPT condition (own ideas first vs LLM first; unusual vs copied prompt) and correlations between number of prompts and number of ideas (r(32)=.43, p=.008), weighted uniqueness (r(32)=.46, p=.004), and homogeneity (r(32)=.23, p=.185); these are not randomized contrasts and are not listed as outcomes. Table 1 (PDF p. 7) reports interview themes, not scored outcomes. Appendix A Table 2 (PDF p. 13) validates embedding models against human categories (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 average 58.92%). Paper does not evaluate idea quality and uses no human creativity ratings. The d values are printed by the paper; their standardizer is not stated.
